intro.opening: A long day north on the desert highway to the city Alexander founded in 331 BC. Almost none of ancient Alexandria is visible above ground, so the day reads what survives: the Catacombs of Kom el-Shoqafa, Pompey's Pillar, the Greco-Roman Museum and the Roman amphitheatre at Kom el-Dikka. Back in Cairo by evening.
intro.whyThisOrder: The modern city was built directly over the ancient one, and what survives is what was underground, too heavy to move, excavated below street level, or collected since. Four sites tell one story about a city's afterlife. The drive is roughly 220 kilometres each way, around two and a half to three hours in normal traffic, so the day starts early and reaches Alexandria mid-morning.
intro.returnNote: Drop-off at your hotel in Cairo in the evening.
fitFor: are reading Egypt's Greco-Roman and late-antique chapter, the city that survives mostly underground
worthKnowing: It's about 13 hours, and as a day-return from Cairo it's genuinely long.
The drive is around two and a half to three hours each way in normal traffic.

intro.closingLine: One long day from Cairo is enough to read what is left.

periods.periodLabel: The drive north and Kom el-Shoqafa

stops.title: Early departure from Cairo
stops.text: An early start on the Cairo-Alexandria Desert Highway, roughly 220 kilometres, around two and a half to three hours in normal traffic, in an air-conditioned vehicle. The schedule allows arrival in Alexandria mid-morning.

stops.title: The Catacombs of Kom el-Shoqafa
stops.text: The largest known Greco-Roman burial complex in Egypt, found in 1900 when a donkey fell through a collapsed passage, cut into bedrock on three descending levels. Egyptian funerary deities, Anubis, Sobek and Thoth, are rendered in Hellenistic and Roman style, including the famous panel of Anubis in Roman armour.

stops.title: Pompey's Pillar and the Serapeum
stops.text: A 26.85-metre monolithic column of red Aswan granite, erected in 297 AD in honour of the Emperor Diocletian; the name is a medieval mistake. It marks the centre of the destroyed Serapeum, the temple of Serapis. The temple was destroyed in 391 AD; the column survived.

stops.title: The Greco-Roman Museum
stops.text: Objects from roughly 300 BC through the seventh century AD: portrait sculpture, terracotta figurines, papyrus fragments, coins, sarcophagi. The museum has had phased restoration; your guide will tell you which galleries are open on the day.

stops.title: The Roman Amphitheatre at Kom el-Dikka
stops.text: The only excavated Roman-period theatre in Egypt, built in the fourth century AD, with thirteen tiers of white marble seating around a small orchestra. Around it, Roman housing, bath complexes and lecture halls: the actual texture of late antique Alexandria.
